finding.claim: SQL injection in /search: the q query parameter is interpolated into the SQL string with an f-string, so an attacker can alter the query, e.g. read other tables with UNION or bypass the filter.
finding.source: request.args.get('q') at app.py:11, an unauthenticated HTTP query parameter
finding.sink: db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'") at app.py:12

trace.note: Route /search is exposed with no authentication
term = request.args.get('q', '') is taken directly from the request
term is formatted into the SQL text with an f-string and executed; the result is returned via jsonify at line 13

finding.guards_checked: No parameterization on this query; the other routes (lines 18 and 25) use ? placeholders, but this one does not. No input validation, escaping, auth or WAF found in the 27-line app. Flask does not sanitize query strings. sqlite3 execute() refuses multiple statements, so stacked queries are not possible, but UNION-based extraction and boolean/error-based injection still work. Example: q=' UNION SELECT id, sql FROM sqlite_master--

verdict.reason: app.py:11 reads the unauthenticated q parameter and app.py:12 puts it into the SQL string with an f-string, with no placeholder, validation or auth (the route decorator is at line 9 and the def at line 10, a trivial offset), so UNION-based injection works, though sqlite3 blocks stacked statements.

verdict_facts.reason: app.py:11-12 takes request.args.get('q') from the unauthenticated /search route (line 9) and puts it into the SQL text with an f-string. There is no parameterization, allowlist, auth decorator or validation, so UNION-based injection works, and the other routes' placeholders (lines 18 and 25) do not protect this one.
